code.title: String never changes: methods return new objects

followUps:
Make the class final, make every field private final, give no setters, and copy any mutable input or output. That way no code can change an object after the constructor finishes.

The copy step matters. If you store a Date or List passed in by the caller, the caller can still change it. Copy on the way in and on the way out:

public final class Booking {
  private final List<String> seats;
  public Booking(List<String> s) { seats = List.copyOf(s); }
  public List<String> seats() { return seats; }
}

Since Java 16 a record does most of this for you, except the defensive copies.

No. final only stops you from pointing the variable at a different object; the StringBuilder it points to can still change.

For example final StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("ab"); sb.append("c"); works and sb now holds "abc". Only sb = new StringBuilder(); is a compile error. Immutability is a property of the class (no method changes its state), not of the variable. StringBuilder is mutable by design, so a final reference to it is a constant reference to a changing object.

The cost is extra objects: every change makes a new String, so repeated changes create garbage and copy characters. Java reduces this in several ways.

  • The String pool shares one object for equal literals.
  • StringBuilder gives a mutable buffer for loops: 1000 appends cost about 1000 steps, while 1000 += copy roughly 500,000 characters.
  • The hash code is cached.
  • Compact strings store Latin-1 text in 1 byte per char, and G1 can deduplicate equal strings.

The gain is safety: sharing, no locks and reliable map keys.

code.title: == versus equals on Strings

followUps:
Almost never for Strings; the honest cases are comparing against a value you know is interned, or checking identity on purpose. The main legitimate use is s == null.

Beyond null, == on Strings works only by accident of the pool: "a" == "a" is true but new String("a") == "a" is false. A fast-path like if (s == other) return true; inside an equals method is fine because equals still handles the false case. Enum constants and interned values can use ==, but a code reviewer will still ask you to use equals.

equalsIgnoreCase treats upper and lower case as the same letter, so "Java".equalsIgnoreCase("JAVA") is true while equals gives false.

It compares char by char and, if two chars differ, tries both Character.toUpperCase and toLowerCase of each before giving up. It is not locale-aware, so it is safe from the Turkish dotless-i problem that toLowerCase() without a locale can cause. It returns false for null and for different lengths. Use it for case-insensitive keywords such as HTTP header names, not for user-visible sorting.

contentEquals compares a String with any CharSequence, such as a StringBuilder or StringBuffer, by text content.

Plain equals returns false when the argument is not a String: "ab".equals(new StringBuilder("ab")) is false, while "ab".contentEquals(new StringBuilder("ab")) is true. It saves you a toString() copy of the builder. The comparison is O(n) in the text length, and for a StringBuffer it locks the buffer while it compares.

code.title: String pool and intern()

followUps:
The answer is usually one pooled String plus one new heap String, and the pooled one is created only if "abc" was not already in the pool.

The literal "abc" is resolved to the pool when the class first runs that instruction (object 1, if new). Then new always allocates a fresh String (object 2). So the count is 2 on first use and 1 afterwards. Counting the internal byte[] arrays, the new String shares the same array as the pooled one, so no third object is made in modern JDKs.

Before Java 7 the pool lived in PermGen, a fixed-size area that was not collected like the normal heap. Interning many unique strings kept filling it until it ran out.

For example, interning ten million distinct user IDs would add ten million permanent entries, and -XX:MaxPermSize (often 64 to 256 MB) was exceeded, giving OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space. Since Java 7 the pool is on the normal heap, so unreferenced interned strings can be garbage collected, and since Java 8 PermGen no longer exists (Metaspace replaced it). Heavy interning is still slower than a HashMap, though.

intern() makes you look up a canonical object yourself in one global table; deduplication works silently inside the garbage collector and keeps the String objects but shares their arrays.

With -XX:+UseStringDeduplication (G1, ZGC and others), the GC finds Strings with equal content and makes them point to one byte[]. The String objects remain different, so == still returns false. Intern changes which String object you hold, so == becomes true. Deduplication needs no code change and saves memory only; intern needs code and gives identity comparison.

code.title: How many objects does new String("hello") make?

followUps:
The expression gives false: new String("hello") == "hello" compares two different objects.

The left side is a fresh heap object, the right side is the pooled literal. Their content is equal, so equals is true, but they are separate objects with different identities. The only way to make them the same object is to call intern() on the new String, which hands back the pooled one. That is why compare with equals, not ==, and avoid new String("...") in normal code.

It gives true, because intern() returns the pooled instance and the literal "hello" is that same pooled instance.

The new String is a separate heap object. intern() looks in the pool, finds the entry for "hello" (the literal puts it there when the class loads), and returns that pooled reference, not the new copy. So both sides of == are the same object. If the pool had no "hello" yet, intern() would add the new String itself, and the result would still be true.

code.title: += in a loop versus StringBuilder

followUps:
Each += builds a brand new String and copies all the old characters, so n appends cost about n squared over 2 character copies, not n.

For 10,000 appends of one char that is about 50 million copied chars. Even if javac turns one a + b + c expression into a StringBuilder or invokedynamic call, it does so for that single expression. In a loop each iteration still makes a fresh builder, appends the whole old string, then calls toString() again, copying everything twice. Keep one StringBuilder outside the loop.

No, StringBuilder does not override equals or hashCode, so it uses identity from Object.

Two builders holding "ab" are not equal: new StringBuilder("ab").equals(new StringBuilder("ab")) is false. This also makes a builder a bad HashMap key. To compare text use sb.toString().equals(...), s.contentEquals(sb), or sb.compareTo(other), which StringBuilder has had since Java 11.

Pick one of two ways: give each thread its own StringBuilder and join the results, or use StringBuffer or a lock when many threads must append to one shared buffer.

Per-thread builders need no locking, so they are fastest; for example 4 threads each build a part, and one thread joins them. StringBuffer makes each single call safe, but two calls in a row (append(a); append(b)) can interleave with another thread's. If order matters, hold one lock around the whole sequence, or collect lines in a ConcurrentLinkedQueue and build one string at the end.

code.title: StringBuilder capacity growth

followUps:
The default capacity of new StringBuilder() is 16 characters; new StringBuilder(String s) gives s.length() + 16.

So new StringBuilder("hello") has capacity 21. The length is how many chars you have written, and the capacity is how many fit before the array must be replaced. When the 17th char arrives in an empty builder, the capacity becomes 16 * 2 + 2 = 34, then 70, then 142.

It does not create a builder holding "a"; it calls StringBuilder(int capacity), because a char widens to int 97.

The result is an empty builder with capacity 97 and length 0, so toString() gives an empty string. This is a classic trap. To start with the letter use new StringBuilder("a") or new StringBuilder().append('a'). The wasted capacity is small here, but with 'z' (122) the difference is still harmless; with a char from a large Unicode range it can waste up to about 65 K chars.

trimToSize() shrinks the internal array down to the current length, so no spare space is kept.

If a builder has length 50 and capacity 142, calling it allocates a new array of 50 and copies the data once. This helps when you keep a builder for a long time after finishing writing. It is only a hint to the JVM and may do nothing. Usually you call toString() and drop the builder instead, which already makes an exact-size String.

code.title: Wrapper classes: generics, null and utilities

followUps:
parseInt returns a primitive int, while valueOf returns an Integer object (from the cache for -128 to 127).

Both throw NumberFormatException for bad text like "abc" or "". Use parseInt("42") when you want arithmetic and valueOf("42") when you need an object, for example to put it in a list. Mixing them just causes extra boxing or unboxing: Integer x = Integer.parseInt(s) boxes once, which is fine, but int y = Integer.valueOf(s) creates an object and then unboxes it.

They were deprecated because new Integer(5) always allocates a new object, wasting memory and breaking the cache, while Integer.valueOf(5) can reuse one.

They are marked deprecated for removal since Java 9 (finalised in Java 16 as a warning). Value-based classes should be compared by value, and the language wants to let the JVM treat wrappers like values in the future (Project Valhalla). Using new Integer(5) == new Integer(5) is always false, which is a trap. Use Integer.valueOf or just autoboxing.

About 20 MB or more for one million Integers, against about 4 MB for an int[] of the same size.

The ArrayList holds a reference per element (4 bytes with compressed pointers, 8 without) so about 4 MB for the array, and each Integer object adds roughly 16 bytes (12 header plus 4 value) for another 16 MB. Values -128 to 127 are shared, so only large values cost extra. Allocation and cache misses also slow loops down. Use int[] or a primitive collection library when size matters.

code.title: Autoboxing pitfalls

followUps:
The cache covers -128 to 127 by default, and yes, the upper bound can be raised with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=N (or -Djava.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high=N in older JDKs).

The lower bound -128 is fixed. The Java Language Specification guarantees only that range, so another JVM could cache more. For example with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=2000, Integer a = 1000, b = 1000; a == b becomes true. That is a good reason never to rely on it: your code would behave differently depending on a flag.

Float and Double have no cache at all, because there are too many possible values to share.

So Double a = 1.0, b = 1.0; a == b is false in practice. The others do cache: Byte (all 256 values), Short, Integer and Long (-128 to 127), Character (0 to 127), and Boolean (TRUE and FALSE). BigInteger and BigDecimal are not wrappers, but BigInteger.ZERO, ONE and TEN are shared constants.

The line int n = map.get("missing"); throws a NullPointerException, because get returns a null Integer that is unboxed.

Another form is Integer x = null; int y = x + 1;, where x + 1 calls x.intValue() implicitly. A third is Integer none = null; if (none == 0), since comparing an Integer with an int unboxes the Integer first. There is no visible dot-call in any of these, which is why the bug is easy to miss.

code.title: The Integer cache

followUps:
The range is small because those values are used the most (loop counters, small flags, bytes), so caching them saves the most allocations for a tiny fixed memory cost.

The range -128 to 127 equals the range of a signed byte, which is 256 objects of about 16 bytes, about 4 KB. Caching all four billion ints would take about 64 GB. A bigger range would slow startup and waste memory for values that most programs never use, which is why the bound is only a tunable option.

The result is false, because each new Integer(100) bypasses the cache and allocates a new object.

Both sides are different objects, so the reference comparison fails even though the value 100 is inside the cached range. equals would return true. This is the reason the constructors are deprecated: they make caching unreliable. Integer.valueOf(100) == Integer.valueOf(100) is true, but you still should not depend on it.

No, not in normal code: compare wrappers with equals, or unbox one side first.

The cache is an optimisation the language only partly promises, so code that works for 100 and breaks for 1000 is a latent bug. Tests with small numbers will pass, then production IDs above 127 fail. The fix is a.equals(b), Objects.equals(a, b), or a.intValue() == b.intValue(). The only place this matters is in puzzles and interviews, where you explain why it prints false.

code.title: Breaking the equals/hashCode contract

followUps:
HashMap first takes key.hashCode() to find the bucket, then uses equals to find the right key inside that bucket.

Steps for get(k): compute the hash and spread it, pick index = hash & (n - 1), then walk that bucket. A node matches if its stored hash is equal and the key is the same object or k.equals(nodeKey). If the hashCode is wrong the lookup goes to the wrong bucket and misses. If equals is wrong, you find the right bucket but never match. Average cost is O(1).

getClass() requires exactly the same class, which keeps equals symmetric; instanceof accepts subclasses, which is more flexible but can break symmetry.

Example: Point equals uses instanceof, and ColorPoint extends Point adds a colour. Then point.equals(colorPoint) is true but colorPoint.equals(point) is false. With getClass() both are false, which is consistent. Use instanceof with a final class (or a record), where no subclass exists, and getClass() otherwise.

Use a library like EqualsVerifier, or write property tests that check each rule on many generated objects.

For example, for random objects a, b and c, assert a.equals(a), that a.equals(b) == b.equals(a), that equal objects have equal hash codes, and that a.equals(null) is false. EqualsVerifier.forClass(Point.class).verify(); checks all of this, including missing fields and mutability. Also add a plain test that puts an object in a HashSet and finds it with an equal copy.

code.title: HashMap bucket index from hashCode

followUps:
Because then the bucket index can be found with a fast bit mask, hash & (n - 1), instead of a slow division with remainder.

If n is 16 then n - 1 is binary 1111, so the mask keeps the low 4 bits, which equals hash % 16 for non-negative numbers. Doubling the table also keeps things simple: each node either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity, so resizing only needs to test one bit per node. For n = 16, hash 21 (10101) goes to bucket 5.

Because the index uses only the low bits of the hash, so differences in the high bits would be ignored and cause many collisions.

The step h ^ (h >>> 16) mixes the top 16 bits into the bottom 16. Take hashes 0x10000 and 0x20000: with a table of 16 both would land in bucket 0 without spreading. After spreading they go to buckets 1 and 2. It costs one shift and one XOR, so it is almost free.

Treeified buckets need to compare keys, so keys that implement Comparable let the tree be ordered and give O(log n) lookups instead of a slow scan.

When a bucket has 8 or more nodes and the table has 64 or more slots, the nodes become a red-black tree ordered by hash. If many keys share one hash, HashMap falls back to compareTo when keys are Comparable of the same class; if they are not, it may have to search both subtrees, which approaches O(n). That is why user-controlled keys should be Comparable.

code.title: Comparable versus Comparator

followUps:
TreeSet uses the comparator (or compareTo), not equals: two elements are duplicates when the comparison returns 0.

So a TreeSet with comparator by string length treats "cat" and "dog" as the same element and keeps only the first. A HashSet would keep both because their equals is false. This is why the comparator should be consistent with equals, or the set will not behave like a normal Set. Operations cost O(log n), against about O(1) for a HashSet.

Chain the comparators: sort by the first key descending, then use thenComparing for the second key ascending.

people.sort(
  Comparator.comparing(Person::age, Comparator.reverseOrder())
            .thenComparing(Person::name));

For ages 30, 41, 30 with names Zoe, Amy, Bob, the result is Amy (41), Bob (30), Zoe (30). Each step only breaks ties left by the one before it.

The compiler cannot work out the type of p in the lambda, because .reversed() is called on the result of comparing(...) before the target type is known.

It infers Object for p, so p.age() fails with "cannot find symbol". Fix it by naming the type, (Person p) -> p.age(), by using a method reference Person::age, or by writing Comparator.comparing(Person::age, Comparator.reverseOrder()).

code.title: Comparator not consistent with equals

followUps:
No. BigDecimal natural ordering (compareTo) ignores scale, while its equals does not, so 1.0 and 1.00 are not consistent.

new BigDecimal("1.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("1.00")) is 0, but equals is false because the scales (1 and 2) differ. The javadoc says so explicitly. So a TreeSet holds one of them and a HashSet holds both. To avoid surprises, normalise with stripTrailingZeros() or setScale(2) before using them as keys.

It can throw IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract! during the sort.

The TimSort algorithm in Collections.sort and List.sort sometimes notices that a, b and c give an impossible cycle (a < b, b < c, but c < a). It is not guaranteed to notice, so a broken comparator may also just produce a wrongly ordered list on small inputs. A typical cause is a comparator that returns only 1 or -1 and never 0, or one that subtracts ints and overflows.

code.title: Immutable key shared by many threads

followUps:
Because a key whose fields change after insertion ends up in the wrong bucket, so the map can no longer find it, even in one thread.

Example: a Point(1,2) is put in with hash 33 and then setX(5) changes its hash to 157. A get(point) now looks in another bucket and returns null, while the entry is still in the map, which is a memory leak. Immutable keys avoid this. Immutability also makes sharing between threads safe with no locks, and lets you cache the hash.

Compute it lazily once, store it in a private field, and rely on the fields being final so the value never goes stale. This is how String does it.

private int hash; // 0 means not computed
public int hashCode() {
  int h = hash;
  if (h == 0) { h = Objects.hash(a, b); hash = h; }
  return h;
}

The race is harmless: two threads may both compute the same value, and an int write is atomic. The field must not be final, and a hash that is truly 0 will just be recomputed each time.

Use the business (natural) key in equals and hashCode if one exists; if only a generated id exists, use a constant hashCode and compare ids only when they are not null.

The problem is that the id is null before save and set after, so a hash based on it changes after the entity is in a HashSet. Safe options: base equality on an immutable unique field such as email or ISBN; or return getClass().hashCode() as a stable value, and in equals treat entities as equal only when both ids are non-null and the same. The constant hash costs speed in big sets, so prefer the business key.
